prompt: Your travel agent needs a weather tool it has never heard of, so it asks a registry that searches sites' tool lists. Which standard is at work?
explain: ARD is a search engine for agent tools: sites publish /.well-known/ard.json and registries collect those files to answer plain-language searches. A high ranking still isn't proof a tool is trustworthy.

prompt: ARD and ai-catalog agreed to stay loosely linked. How do they split the work?
options: They merged into one shared file
explain: ai-catalog is the publishing format, your site's list of its AI offerings; ARD is the discovery format that registries crawl. The practical tip: serve the same file at both ard.json and ai-catalog.json.

prompt: A restaurant lists its booking tool and its jobs tool in one JSON file, like a table of contents for AI. Which standard?
explain: ai-catalog is one JSON list at /.well-known/ai-catalog.json. Like a table of contents, it doesn't hold the tools themselves; each entry says what kind of thing it is and links to its full description or includes it.

prompt: ARD calls ai-catalog its predecessor. True or false: it still pays to serve ai-catalog.json.
explain: ai-catalog was split off, not retired. MCP's Server Cards point discovery at ai-catalog.json and many publishers only use that address, so serve one file at both ai-catalog.json and ard.json.

prompt: Your recipe site answers "vegetarian dinners under 30 minutes, no nuts" at /ask for people and /mcp for agents. Which standard?
explain: NLWeb indexes the structured data a site already has, like Schema.org tags and RSS, and answers only from that site. Every NLWeb site is also an MCP server, so agents can ask the same questions.

prompt: NLWeb has a W3C community group. What does that make NLWeb?
explain: Community groups are open forums that anyone can propose, and they aren't a standards track. W3C standards come out of working groups, so NLWeb is an open spec with a W3C discussion space.

prompt: R.V. Guha helped create RSS and Schema.org. Which two agentic-web standards also carry his name?
explain: Guha conceived NLWeb at Microsoft and co-authored ARD with Google and Hugging Face. NLWeb even reuses his earlier work: it indexes a site's Schema.org data.

prompt: A salon's page calls document.modelContext.registerTool() so the agent in your browser can book_appointment. Which standard?
explain: WebMCP lets a page hand typed tools, with names, descriptions and fields, to the agent in your browser. The agent stops hunting for the calendar widget and just calls the tool.

prompt: When an agent calls a WebMCP tool, where does the work happen?
options: In your own signed-in browser tab
explain: WebMCP tools are JavaScript functions on the page, running in your tab and your session, so you can watch and step in. A regular MCP server serves agents that never load your page.

prompt: WebMCP tools come with plain-English descriptions the AI reads. What's the catch?
options: A shady site can trick the agent
explain: Tool descriptions are text the model reads, so a malicious page can try prompt injection. Chrome says agents must defend against this and gives sites ways to flag untrusted text.

prompt: A news site lets a verified shopping agent in but blocks a scraper wearing the exact same user-agent label. Which standard tells them apart?
explain: With Web Bot Auth, the bot's operator publishes public keys and signs every request. Anyone can copy a label, but nobody can fake a valid signature without the private key.

prompt: Web Bot Auth didn't invent its own crypto. Which existing IETF standard does it sign requests with?
explain: It reuses RFC 9421, HTTP Message Signatures, which signs chosen parts of a request. Web Bot Auth adds where a bot's keys live and how a site finds them.

prompt: True or false: Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol and Mastercard's Agent Pay build on Web Bot Auth.
explain: Both build on Web Bot Auth's signed requests and add a tag saying whether the agent is browsing or buying. The card networks reused the bot ID layer instead of inventing their own.

prompt: Your coding agent calls a scraping API you've never used, gets "401: who are you?" and a file explaining how to sign you up. Which standard?
explain: auth.md is a sign-up page written for robots, served at yourapp.com/auth.md. However the agent signs you up, it ends with a normal short-lived, revocable OAuth token tied to you.

prompt: Spot the fake: which is NOT one of auth.md's ways for an agent to sign you up?
options: Vouched for by the agent's maker
Type a code on the service's page
Pay a $1 fee to prove you're human
explain: auth.md has three paths: the agent's maker vouches for you, you sign in and type a short code on the service's own page, or the agent starts anonymous and you claim the account later. No fee involved.

prompt: It's a valet key for your personal agent: it can sign in and act for you, but can't open the glovebox. Which standard?
explain: Poppy, the Personal Agent Protocol, lets your agent sign in to a company as you, with only the permissions you granted. The company explains how at /.well-known/poppy.json.

prompt: True or false: OpenAI, Visa and PayPal are Poppy design partners, so they already support it.
explain: Design partners help shape a draft; that's not the same as shipping it. Before believing a logo, check whether the company actually serves a poppy.json.

prompt: Spot the fake: which standard is paired with the wrong creators?
explain: Poppy came from Sierra and Meta, announced October 6, 2026. The rest are right: Google and Shopify launched UCP, OpenAI and Stripe launched ACP, and Stripe and Tempo launched MPP.

prompt: A universal power socket for shopping: any assistant plugs into any store, from catalog to cart to checkout. Which standard?
explain: UCP defines the common steps of buying and carries them over ordinary web APIs, MCP or A2A. A store describes what it supports at /.well-known/ucp, and the retailer stays the legal seller.

prompt: True or false: Amazon sits on UCP's technical council, so Amazon sells through UCP.
explain: A council seat isn't a storefront. Companies join councils to shape a spec; whether they deploy it is a separate question you check store by store.

prompt: You want your products shown in ChatGPT with accurate, current prices, and you already use Stripe. Which standard?
explain: ACP comes from OpenAI and Stripe. Merchants push product feeds and promotions so ChatGPT can show current products, prices and comparisons. UCP is the rival built for any assistant.

prompt: ACP launched alongside "Instant Checkout" in ChatGPT. What is its main job today?
explain: In March 2026 OpenAI expanded ACP to product discovery, while checkout moved back to the merchant's side. The headline feature, buying inside the chat, is the part that was scaled back.

prompt: A signed, notarized shopping list with a spending limit the bank can check before paying. Which standard?
explain: AP2 records what you approved as signed "mandates," so the bank and merchant can answer "did a real person agree to this?" It authorizes payments; other rails actually move the money.

prompt: AP2 supports "Human Not Present" purchases. What does that mean?
options: The agent pays with no limits
You pre-sign rules; it buys later
The merchant signs on your behalf
A bot buys with no user at all
explain: You sign the rules up front, say "concert tickets, under $200," and the agent buys later when the conditions are met, even at 3 a.m. The signed limits are what make that safe for the bank.

prompt: Spot the fake: AP2 records your consent in signed mandates. Which one is made up?
explain: AP2 has checkout mandates (open while they hold your limits, closed once they lock exact items and price) and payment mandates for how you pay. There's no refund mandate.

prompt: A research agent opens a pay-as-you-go "session" on Tempo, pays a fraction of a cent per article, and settles the total when it finishes. Which standard?
explain: MPP, from Stripe and Tempo, answers with HTTP 402 like x402 but adds pay-as-you-go "sessions" and subscriptions. Sessions run on stablecoin rails like Tempo; cards through Stripe cover one-off charges.

prompt: MPP's core spec is an "individual" IETF Internet-Draft. What does "individual" tell you?
options: No working group has taken it on
Only one company may use it
explain: Anyone can post an Internet-Draft. An individual draft has no formal standing until a working group adopts it, so "it's at the IETF" isn't the same as "the IETF is standardizing it."

prompt: A parking meter on every web page: drop in a cent of USDC, the gate opens, no account needed. Which standard?
explain: x402, created by Coinbase and now run by a Linux Foundation project, answers with HTTP 402 and a price, and the client attaches a signed stablecoin payment. MPP is the close cousin that also takes cards.

prompt: True or false: Cloudflare sees about a billion 402 responses a day, so x402 handles a billion payments a day.
explain: A 402 is a request for payment, not a payment, and most never get paid. To size x402, count settled dollars, not 402 responses or transaction counts.

prompt: In x402, the client attaches a signed USDC payment. What does the "facilitator" do?
explain: The facilitator checks the payment and settles it on-chain in seconds, so the server doesn't run blockchain plumbing itself. Fees are a fraction of a cent, which card networks can't match.

prompt: HTTP has had a 402 Payment Required code since the 1990s. What does RFC 9110 say it does?
explain: RFC 9110 just says 402 is "reserved for future use," and it sat unused for decades. x402 and MPP finally give it a job: answer with a price and how to pay.

prompt: Where must a site put its robots.txt file?
explain: RFC 9309 says the file must be /robots.txt at the top level. It's older than the /.well-known/ folder (RFC 8615) that newer files like ard.json and poppy.json use.

prompt: True or false: robots.txt rules are a polite request, not a lock.
explain: RFC 9309 says the rules "are not a form of access authorization." Good crawlers follow them; a bot that ignores them isn't stopped, which is why sites want signed bot identity like Web Bot Auth.

prompt: Your TV says "Go to example.com/device and enter WDJB-MJHT." Which OAuth flow is that?
explain: The device authorization grant (RFC 8628) lets a device with no good keyboard get your approval on another screen. Poppy uses the same pattern when you approve an agent on another device with a code.

prompt: PKCE, pronounced "pixy," is added to OAuth's sign-in code flow. What problem does it solve?
explain: The app makes a one-time secret, sends a hashed version at the start, and reveals the secret when trading the code for a token. A thief who grabs the code can't use it without that secret.

prompt: Who introduced the Model Context Protocol (MCP) in November 2024?
explain: Anthropic open-sourced MCP on November 25, 2024 as one standard way to plug AI apps into tools and data. Lots here builds on it: every NLWeb site is an MCP server, and WebMCP borrows its idea of tools.

prompt: Under the hood, what message format do MCP clients and servers speak?
explain: MCP messages are JSON-RPC 2.0: small JSON objects with a method, params and an id. That keeps them simple to carry over a local pipe or over HTTP.

prompt: Spot the fake: MCP servers offer three core building blocks. Which isn't one?
explain: MCP servers expose tools (functions the model can call), resources (data it can read) and prompts (reusable templates). "Actions" sounds right but isn't an MCP building block.

prompt: Google's A2A protocol lets agents talk to agents. Where does an agent publish its Agent Card?
explain: An A2A Agent Card is a JSON file at /.well-known/agent-card.json saying what the agent can do and how to reach it. Google launched A2A in April 2025 and later gave it to the Linux Foundation.

prompt: MCP and A2A get mixed up a lot. What's the usual split?
options: MCP links tools, A2A links agents
MCP links agents, A2A links tools
MCP runs in browsers, A2A servers
explain: MCP connects an AI app to tools and data; A2A lets independent agents find each other and hand off tasks. Google pitched A2A as a complement to MCP, not a replacement.

prompt: Jeremy Howard proposed /llms.txt in September 2024. What's inside it?
options: A Markdown guide to the site
A JSON list of API keys
explain: llms.txt is a Markdown file with a short summary and links to the pages worth reading, so a model finds the good stuff fast. It guides models; it doesn't set rules the way robots.txt does.

prompt: A request says "User-Agent: ChatGPT-User". Why can't a site trust that alone?
explain: A user-agent string is a self-written label, so a scraper can copy it word for word. IP checks break easily too, which is why Web Bot Auth adds cryptographic signatures.

prompt: Sign-in servers publish a JWKS so others can check their signatures. What's in a JWKS?
explain: A JWK Set (RFC 7517) is a JSON object with a "keys" array of public keys. Sharing public keys is safe; the private keys stay with the owner and do the signing.

prompt: x402 payments usually move USDC, a dollar stablecoin. Which company issues USDC?
explain: Circle issues USDC, a token designed to stay worth one US dollar. Coinbase, which created x402, is a major USDC partner, hence the common mix-up.

prompt: Spot the fake: which header is NOT defined by RFC 9421, HTTP Message Signatures?
explain: RFC 9421 defines Signature-Input (what was signed and how), Signature (the signature itself) and Accept-Signature (a server asking for one). Web Bot Auth builds on these.

prompt: Spot the fake CORS header: which one doesn't exist?
explain: CORS headers tell browsers which other sites' scripts may read a response. There's no agent switch: CORS is about browser origins, not bots, so bot identity needs something like Web Bot Auth.

prompt: Spot the fake: three of these OAuth discovery files are registered under /.well-known/. Which is invented?
explain: openid-configuration and oauth-authorization-server describe a sign-in server; oauth-protected-resource (RFC 9728) tells a client which server guards an API. auth.md and MCP lean on these same files.

prompt: Spot the fake HTTP status code: which one isn't in the official registry?
explain: 402, 425 (RFC 8470) and 451 (RFC 7725, a nod to Fahrenheit 451) are all registered. There's no status code for unverified bots; that job falls to signatures, not a new number.
